# **Lab 5: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Overview

In this lab, you will investigate how the **sample mean** behaves when repeated samples are drawn from a population. Each group will work with a different hypothetical population. Your goal is to explore the **sampling distribution** of the sample mean, defined as:

$$\hat{\mu} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i$$

By the end of this lab, you should be able to explain what happens to this distribution as the sample size $n$ increases — this is the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) in action.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The diagram below illustrates the general simulation workflow for this lab.

Choose **one** of the five populations below. Each population has a large size of $N = 100{,}000$ observations, and you will draw samples of size $n = 500$ from it. Note that all populations are designed to share the same standard deviation ($\sigma \approx 0.447$), allowing for fair comparisons across groups.

### Population 1: Normal Distribution

Parameters: $\mu = 2$, $\sigma = 0.447$

```{r pop1-show, eval=FALSE}
sigma <- 0.447
N     <- 100000
n     <- 500
pop   <- rnorm(N, mean = 2, sd = sigma)
```

```{r pop1-plot, echo=FALSE}
sigma <- 0.447
N     <- 100000
n     <- 500
pop   <- rnorm(N, mean = 2, sd = sigma)

data.frame(X = pop) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = X)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(title = "Population 1: Normal Distribution",
       subtitle = paste0("mu = 2, sigma = ", sigma),
       x = "X", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

### Population 2: Bernoulli Distribution

Parameters: $p = 0.3$, so $\sigma = \sqrt{p(1-p)} \approx 0.458$

```{r pop2-show, eval=FALSE}
N     <- 100000
n     <- 500
prob  <- 0.3
pop   <- rbinom(N, size = 1, prob = prob)
sigma <- sd(pop)   # empirical SD of the finite population
```

```{r pop2-plot, echo=FALSE}
N    <- 100000
n    <- 500
prob <- 0.3
pop  <- rbinom(N, size = 1, prob = prob)

data.frame(X = pop) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = X)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(title = "Population 2: Bernoulli Distribution",

       x = "X", y = "Count") +

```

### Population 4: Exponential Distribution

Parameters: rate $= 1/\sigma \approx 2.237$, so the mean $= \sigma \approx 0.447$

```{r pop4-show, eval=FALSE}
sigma      <- 0.447
N          <- 100000
n          <- 500
lambda_exp <- 1 / sigma
pop        <- rexp(N, rate = lambda_exp)
```


### Population 5: Gamma Distribution

Parameters: shape $\alpha = 4$, rate $\beta = \sqrt{\alpha}/\sigma$

```{r pop5-show, eval=FALSE}
sigma       <- 0.447
N           <- 100000
n           <- 500
alpha_gamma <- 4
beta_gamma  <- sqrt(alpha_gamma) / sigma
pop         <- rgamma(N, shape = alpha_gamma, rate = beta_gamma)
```

```{r pop5-plot, echo=FALSE}
sigma       <- 0.447
N           <- 100000
n           <- 500
alpha_gamma <- 4
beta_gamma  <- sqrt(alpha_gamma) / sigma
pop         <- rgamma(N, shape = alpha_gamma, rate = beta_gamma)

data.frame(X = pop) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = X)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(title = "Population 5: Gamma Distribution",
       subtitle = paste0("shape = ", alpha_gamma, ", rate = ", round(beta_gamma, 3)),
       x = "X", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

## Key Concepts to Keep in Mind

Before you start coding, make sure you understand the following ideas. Read through them carefully — they will guide your answers in the reflection section.

### What is a Sampling Distribution?

When you draw a sample of size $n$ from a population and compute the sample mean $\hat{\mu}$, you get **one number**. But if you repeated that process many times (say, $K = 1{,}000$ times), you would get $K$ different values of $\hat{\mu}$. The distribution of those $K$ values is called the **sampling distribution of the sample mean**.

> **Key idea:** A sampling distribution is not the distribution of the data — it is the distribution of a *statistic* (here, the mean) computed from repeated samples.

### What does the Central Limit Theorem say?

The **Central Limit Theorem (CLT)** states that, regardless of the shape of the original population, the sampling distribution of $\hat{\mu}$ approaches a **Normal distribution** as $n$ increases. More precisely:

$$\hat{\mu} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu,\; \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right) \quad \text{as } n \to \infty$$

This means:

- The **center** of the sampling distribution equals the population mean $\mu$.
- The **spread** (standard deviation) of the sampling distribution equals $\sigma / \sqrt{n}$, called the **Standard Error (SE)**.
- The **shape** becomes bell-shaped (Normal) as $n$ grows, even if the population is skewed or discrete.

### Distinguishing $n$ from $K$

It is easy to confuse these two quantities:

| Symbol | Meaning | Effect when increased |
|----|----|----|
| $n$ | Sample size (observations per sample) | Reduces the spread of $\hat{\mu}$; makes the sampling distribution narrower and more Normal |
| $K$ | Number of repeated samples | Gives a more accurate *picture* of the sampling distribution; does not change its true shape or spread |

> **Analogy:** $n$ controls how precise each estimate is. $K$ controls how well you can see the distribution of those estimates.

### The 68–95–99.7 Rule (Empirical Rule)

For a Normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$:

- About **68%** of values fall within $\pm 1$ standard deviation of the mean.
- About **95%** fall within $\pm 2$ standard deviations.
- About **99.7%** fall within $\pm 3$ standard deviations.

You will use this rule in Question 6 to check whether your sampling distribution is "close enough" to Normal.

### 6. Finding the Minimum $n$ for Approximate Normality

Set $K = 5{,}000$. Using the **68–95–99.7 Empirical Rule**, find the smallest value of $n$ for which the sampling distribution of $\hat{\mu}$ is approximately normal. Specifically, find $n$ such that the observed proportions within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations each differ from the theoretical values (68%, 95%, 99.7%) by less than 0.005.

Let `rate1`, `rate2`, and `rate3` be the proportions of $\hat{\mu}$ values falling within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations of the mean of the $\hat{\mu}$ vector, respectively. The test passes when:

``` r
all(abs(c(rate1 - 0.68, rate2 - 0.95, rate3 - 0.997)) < 0.005)
```

```{r q6}
K <- 5000
# Try different values of n and check the empirical rule

mu_hats <- get_mu_hats(pop, n = ???, K = K)  # Change n values
m  <- mean(mu_hats)
s  <- sd(mu_hats)
rate1 <- mean(abs(mu_hats - m) < 1 * s)
rate2 <- mean(abs(mu_hats - m) < 2 * s)
rate3 <- mean(abs(mu_hats - m) < 3 * s)
all(abs(c(rate1 - 0.68, rate2 - 0.95, rate3 - 0.997)) < 0.005)

```

### 7. Standard Error vs. Empirical Standard Deviation

The **Standard Error (SE)** of the sample mean is the theoretical standard deviation of the sampling distribution:

$$SE = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$

Using $n = 1{,}000$ and $K = 1{,}000$, compute the SE using the formula above and compare it to the standard deviation of your `mu_hats` vector. Are they close? How large does the sample size need to be for them to be close?

Then, compare your SE with other groups. Since all populations were designed to have the same $\sigma$, what would you expect? What do you actually find?

```{r q7}
n <- 10 # change n=100, n=500, n=1000 ...
K <- 1000

# sigma is defined when you set up your population above
SE           <- sigma / sqrt(n)
mu_hats      <- get_mu_hats(pop, n = n, K = K)
empirical_sd <- sd(mu_hats)

SE
empirical_sd
abs(SE - empirical_sd)   # How close are they?
```
